commitResults.messageTitle: Fill in personal details in AGENT.md
commitResults.messageBody:
The template requires self-assessed ratings before the first
increment. Rated 4/5 for both programming and IDE experience
based on prior Java coursework.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename chatbot from Duke to Thomas
commitResults.messageBody:
Rename Duke.java to Thomas.java: a public class must live in file matching its name, so the class and file rename together. Regenerate the start-up banner as well, since the old ASCII art spelled out Duke literally and a textual renam would have left it contradicting the new name. The replacement uses figlet's slant font.

Update both READMEs to match. README.md documents the expected program output as a setup verification step, so leaving the old banner there would have told readers to expect output the program no longer produces.

commitResults.messageTitle: Thomas.java: Greet the user and exit
commitResults.messageBody:
The increment requires the chatbot to print a greeting and then
terminate, with no interaction in between.

Print the greeting and farewell inside the divider lines the spec
shows, placing the start-up banner within the first block rather than
above it, so the banner reads as part of the chatbot's output rather
than as separate program noise.

Extract DIVIDER as a constant. The rule already appears three times and
every later increment adds more, so a single definition removes the
risk of miscounting its underscores.

Keep the greeting and farewell as separate strings even though they are
printed together, since the command loop added next belongs between
them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Thomas.java: Echo user commands until bye
commitResults.messageBody:
The increment requires the chatbot to read commands from the user,
echo each one back, and exit on the command bye.

Read input with a Scanner over System.in, using nextLine rather than
next so that multi-word commands arrive intact. Later increments parse
arguments out of the line, which next would have already split apart.

Loop on hasNextLine rather than while (true). nextLine throws
NoSuchElementException when the input ends, so a loop that relies
solely on the bye break crashes whenever stdin closes first, as it
does under Ctrl-D and when commands are piped in from a file. Asking
hasNextLine first gives the program two clean exits instead of one
clean exit and one stack trace.

Indent output to match the sample: dividers four spaces, text five.
The divider's indent is baked into DIVIDER so call sites never have to
remember the one-space offset, while the text indent is a separate
INDENT constant since the two values differ. Prefixing INDENT to each
banner line leaves the ASCII art itself untouched and re-pastable.

Print the farewell with print rather than println. Every block already
ends in an explicit \n, so println appended a second newline and left
a blank line after the closing divider. Keeping the newline inside the
strings also holds the output to LF on every platform, since println
would emit CRLF on Windows.

commitResults.messageTitle: Thomas.java: Store tasks and list them on request
commitResults.messageBody:
The increment requires the chatbot to store whatever text the user
enters and display it back on the list command, with a fixed-size
array and an assumed ceiling of 100 tasks.

Read input with a Scanner over System.in, using nextLine rather than
next so that multi-word tasks arrive intact. Loop on hasNextLine
rather than while (true): nextLine throws NoSuchElementException at
end of input, so a loop relying solely on the bye break crashes
whenever stdin closes first, as it does under Ctrl-D and when commands
are piped in from a file.

Keep the tasks in a String[MAX_TASKS] with a separate count rather
than a collection, per the increment's stated assumption. Reject
additions past the ceiling with a message, so exceeding it reports a
limit rather than throwing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Extract printBlock to wrap lines in dividers and indent them. The
divider literal had spread to five call sites across three branches,
with two competing styles: some branches built a string and printed it
once, the list branch printed line by line. Routing every block
through one varargs method removes both the duplication and the
inconsistency, and gives the farewell the opening divider it was
missing.

Indent output to match the sample: dividers four spaces, text five.
The divider's indent is baked into DIVIDER so call sites never have to
remember the one-space offset, while the text indent is a separate
INDENT constant since the two values differ.

commitResults.messageTitle: Thomas.java: Mark tasks as done or not done
commitResults.messageBody:
Introduce a Task class that holds a description and a completion flag,
replacing the plain String[] used to store tasks. Task owns its display
format in toString(), so callers never assemble the status icon and text
themselves and a future task type can override it in one place.

Thomas now splits each command on the first space, so `mark <n>` and
`unmark <n>` can flip the completion state of a stored task and echo it
back. Wrap the Scanner in try-with-resources so it is closed when the
loop ends, and fix the greeting/farewell to say "Choo Choo".

commitResults.messageTitle: Thomas.java: Add todo, deadline and event task types
commitResults.messageBody:
Thomas previously stored every line as a plain task. It now recognises
three add commands and stores a distinct task type for each:

* todo <description>
* deadline <description> /by <when>
* event <description> /from <start> /to <end>

TodoTask, DeadlineTask and EventTask extend Task, each overriding
toString() to prepend its [T]/[D]/[E] tag and append its own date fields.
Inheritance keeps the shared description and done-state in one place, and
the existing Task[] can hold all three because list, mark and unmark only
ever call Task methods -- polymorphism picks the right toString() at
print time.

Dates are kept as the raw text the user typed rather than being parsed,
as the level only requires them to be echoed back; parsing is a later
increment.

The acknowledgement changes from "added: <line>" to the "Got it. I've
added this task:" block with a running task count, shared by all three
commands via printAddedBlock(). A line that is not a recognised command
is now ignored instead of being stored, since every task type now has an
explicit keyword.

Also adds test/ui-test-plan.md and the test-ui skill that runs it, so the
console output of each command is checked end to end rather than by hand.
The plan's expected outputs use the new acknowledgement wording.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Require the UI test suite to be run after code changes
commitResults.messageBody:
The text-UI test plan and the test-ui skill that runs it exist, but
nothing told an agent to use them, so they were only run when asked for
by name and the plan drifted behind the code.

State the expectation directly: after any change under src/, update
test/ui-test-plan.md and run the suite before calling the change done.

The two rules that make the suite worth running are spelled out rather
than left implied. Expected output must be derived from the source, as
output pasted from a run agrees with the code by construction and would
pass even when the code is wrong. Failures must be reported as a
transcript and left unfixed, so a regression is visible instead of being
quietly repaired in the same breath. Purely non-observable changes are
exempted so the rule stays credible for comments and renames.

commitResults.messageTitle: Thomas.java: Report invalid commands instead of crashing
commitResults.messageBody:
Thomas previously trusted whatever the user typed. A command missing its
argument indexed past the end of the split line, a non-numeric task
number reached Integer.parseInt, and an out-of-range one indexed the
task array directly, so `todo`, `mark abc` and `mark 9` each ended the
session with a stack trace. An unrecognised command was silently ignored.

Add ThomasException to represent a command the chatbot cannot carry out,
and catch it inside the read loop so an error ends that command alone and
the next one is still read. It extends Exception rather than
RuntimeException: as a checked exception the compiler refuses to build a
call that neither handles nor declares it, which is the guarantee that no
user mistake reaches the user as a stack trace. Its message is written to
be read by the person typing, so each throw site says what was wrong and
what to type instead.

Validate before indexing, in every command:

* todo, deadline and event reject a missing or whitespace-only
  description. The length check alone is not enough, as "todo    " splits
  into two parts rather than one, so isBlank() covers the rest.
* deadline requires text on both sides of /by, and event requires both
  /from and /to. The value after a marker is checked too, since a marker
  can be present with nothing following it.
* mark and unmark require a number, and trim it before parsing so a
  trailing space is not mistaken for a non-numeric argument. The
  NumberFormatException from parseInt is caught and rethrown as a
  ThomasException, so the loop has one kind of user error to report.
* An unrecognised keyword is now reported rather than ignored.

Check the task number against taskCount rather than tasks.length. Every
slot up to 100 is in bounds for the array but holds null until something
is stored, so checking the array length let `mark 9` through to fail
later with a NullPointerException rather than a message.

Split the event markers one at a time rather than on " /from | /to "
together. The combined split matched the two markers in either order, so
"/to 4pm /from 2pm" silently stored the start and end reversed; splitting
in sequence rejects it, and reports which marker is missing.

Move the MAX_TASKS check into the add commands. At the top of the chain
it answered every unrecognised command with a full-list message, and it
has no bearing on list, mark, unmark or bye.

Match bye and list on the command keyword like every other command,
rather than on the whole input line. A trailing space is invisible when
typed, so `bye ` and `list ` were reported as unknown commands while
`mark 1 ` and `todo a ` worked, and the two commands that most need to
be reliable were the two that failed.

Prefix the list with "Here are the tasks in your list:" to match the
sample output, sizing the display array one longer to hold it. The header
shifts every task one place along, so entry i shows task i - 1 numbered
i; an array still sized to taskCount left no room for the header and
threw on the empty list, before anything could be printed. Report the
running count as "task(s)" so a single task no longer reads as "1 tasks".

Extend the test plan to 30 cases. The five that added tasks by typing a
bare description now use todo, as that is an error rather than an add;
TC2's aim changes with them, since the behaviour it named no longer
exists. New cases cover each rejection, and interleave valid and invalid
commands so that a later list would expose an error path that corrupted
the task list or its count.

commitResults.messageTitle: Thomas.java: Delete tasks, and hold them in an ArrayList
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a delete command that removes a task by its number, echoes back the
task it removed so the user can see what went, and reports the new size
of the list. It validates its argument exactly as mark and unmark do: a
missing, non-numeric or out-of-range number is reported and removes
nothing.

Replace the Task[] and its separate taskCount with an ArrayList<Task>.
The array was sized once at 100 and carried a running count beside it,
which deletion would have made awkward: removing a task from the middle
of an array means shuffling every later element down by hand and
decrementing the count, with the two able to drift apart if either is
missed. ArrayList.remove() does the shuffle itself and returns the task
it took out, which is also what the acknowledgement needs to print.

Dropping the separate count removes the possibility of it disagreeing
with the list. Every place that asked for taskCount now asks the list for
its size(), so the number reported to the user, the number the range
checks compare against, and the number of tasks actually stored cannot
diverge.

This drops the 100-task ceiling and the "Sorry, I can only remember 100
tasks!" message with it. An ArrayList grows as tasks are added, so there
is no longer a limit to enforce or to report.

The add commands now build the task into a local before appending it,
keeping the existing property that a command which throws while parsing
its arguments leaves the list untouched.

Extend the test plan to 36 cases. The new ones cover deleting from the
middle, from the end of the list down to empty, and from an empty list,
along with each way the argument can be wrong. Three of them exist for
the state that deletion disturbs: that the tasks after a deleted one are
renumbered, that a task added afterwards continues from the shortened
count rather than one that only grows, and that a task's done state
travels with the task rather than staying on its old number.

commitResults.messageTitle: Thomas.java: Remove duplication from command dispatch and parsing
commitResults.messageBody:
Two kinds of repetition had built up as commands were added. Neither
changes what the chatbot does, so this commit changes no behaviour: the
36 text-UI cases pass unchanged.

The command a user typed was carried as a String and compared against
eight literals in nine equals calls, with todo and deadline each tested
twice because the add commands were grouped and then re-dispatched. A
misspelt literal compiled into a branch that could never run, and no
single place decided whether a word was a command at all.

Add a Command enum naming the eight commands, each holding the word the
user types. The keyword is a field rather than being derived from name(),
so what the user types stays independent of what the constant is called.
Command.fromKeyword is now the one place that decides whether a word is a
command, replacing the trailing else that reported unknown input, so
every case in the dispatch handles a command that really exists.

Dispatch with a switch over the enum. The three add commands share one
case label, so appending and announcing a new task stays written once.

Label the read loop and exit it with break readLoop from the BYE case. A
plain break inside a switch leaves the switch rather than the loop, so
the session would have carried on reading after a bye -- a mistake that
compiles cleanly and produces no warning.

Add a default that throws AssertionError. A switch statement over an enum
is not checked for exhaustiveness, unlike a switch expression, so a
constant added to Command but not handled here would silently do nothing
at all: no output, no error. It cannot be reached from user input, as
fromKeyword rejects any word that is not a constant.

Separately, the guard rejecting a command given without an argument was
written out six times, and mark, unmark and delete each carried their own
copy of the same four steps: require an argument, parse it as an integer,
check it against the number of stored tasks, and convert the user's
1-based number to a 0-based index.

Extract requireArgument and parseTaskIndex. requireArgument returns the
argument rather than only checking it, so the indexing into parts happens
once instead of six callers reaching back for parts[1] after asking
whether it exists. parseTaskIndex builds on it and reduces the three
index commands to a single line each.

Three things previously written three times are now written once: the
minus one that converts the task number, the NumberFormatException caught
and rethrown as a ThomasException, and the range check against the number
of tasks that exist. That last one is why mark 9 reports an error rather
than failing with a NullPointerException, so a fourth copy getting it
wrong would have reintroduced a bug that was fixed deliberately.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add feature to save task list on hard disk
commitResults.messageBody:
Whenever users start a new session, they might want
to reload their tasklist from the previous session.
To achieve this, the task list must be saved in an external file.

What is added:
1. When users add a task, the entire task list is copied to the external
file
2. When users delete a task, the entire task list is copied to the
external file

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
Understand dates and times instead of storing them as text
commitResults.messageBody:
A deadline's /by and an event's /from and /to were kept as whatever the
user typed. That is enough to echo back, but it is not a date: the
chatbot could not tell 2019-12-02 from "no idea :-p", could not show a
date any way other than the way it was typed, and could not answer a
question like "what is due on Thursday" without re-reading the text every
time.

Store them as LocalDateTime instead. A date and a 24-hour time are both
required, in the form 2019-12-02 1800.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add an on command, and tighten how deadlines and events are checked
commitResults.messageBody:
Add "on 2019-12-02", listing the tasks that fall on a day. Each task is
asked whether it falls on the day, through Task.occursOn, rather than
being asked what type it is. An event covers every day it spans, ends
included, so its version is a range test rather than a match against the
start. Matches are numbered by list position, not 1, 2, 3, because those
numbers are what mark and delete take. parseDay is separate from
parseDate because a day takes no time of day, and DATE_DISPLAY_DAY is
separate from DATE_DISPLAY_FORMAT because a LocalDate has no hour to
format.

Fix two mistakes in the command handling. "deadline /by ..." blamed the
missing marker when the description was what was missing: the separator
carries a leading space, and the trimmed argument leaves none in front of
the marker for it to match. And an event was never checked for running
backwards, so one ending before it started was accepted. Reject that in
EventTask's constructor, which the save file is loaded through too, so
such a line is skipped rather than loaded. Equal times stay allowed.

Text-UI test plan: 58 cases pass, up from 48, with ten new cases and no
existing expected output changed. Also correct the "Not yet covered"
section, which still claimed mark 9 crashes the chatbot -- covered by
TC17 since error handling was added -- and explained a save file
guarantee in terms of LocalDate. Case-sensitive keyword matching is added
as the one real gap the audit found.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
Extract user interaction into a Ui class
commitResults.messageBody:
Console reading and writing was spread through Thomas: the printBlock
  helper, the divider and indent constants, the Scanner over standard
  input, and the wording of every message sat alongside the command
  handling, so the read loop could not be followed without stepping over
  formatting code.

  Move all of it into Ui. Fixed messages become named methods, so their
  wording is stated once and the call site says what is being reported
  rather than how it looks. Ui owns the Scanner for the whole session,
  since a second one would buffer ahead and swallow commands.

  Behaviour is unchanged; all 58 text-UI cases pass with the test plan
  untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract save file handling into a Storage class
commitResults.messageBody:
Loading and saving sat in Thomas as four static helpers over a constant
path, so the class that interprets commands also knew the save file
format, opened files and caught IOException. Reading the command loop
meant reading past all of it.

Move that work into Storage, constructed with the path it operates on
rather than reading a constant, so the caller decides where tasks live
and a test can point one at a throwaway file. load() returns the tasks
and save() writes them; both throw rather than printing, since talking
to the user is Ui's job. Lines that cannot be parsed are still skipped
rather than being fatal, but the complaints are now collected and
returned for main to show, instead of Storage reaching for the screen.

parseDate moves to Task, beside the format it reads. Storage and the
command handling both need it, and leaving it in Thomas would have made
Storage depend on its own caller.

Behaviour is unchanged; all 58 text-UI cases pass with the test plan
untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract the task list into a TaskList class
commitResults.messageBody:
The tasks lived in a bare ArrayList that main passed around, so every
caller could index into it directly and the rules about task numbers
had nowhere of their own to live. parseTaskIndex had to be handed a
taskCount to check against, which meant the command layer needed to
know the size of a list it should only have been asking questions of.

Wrap the list in TaskList, exposing only add, get, size, getByNumber,
deleteByNumber and positionsOn. The range check moves there, since only
the list knows how many tasks exist, and parseTaskNumber is left doing
just what its name says. The 1-based to 0-based conversion now happens
in one private method, and the two numbering schemes are told apart by
the method names rather than by the reader's memory.

positionsOn returns the positions of the tasks falling on a day rather
than the tasks themselves, which is what lets Ui keep numbering each
match by its place in the whole list -- the number mark and delete
take. That finishes the split left half-done when Ui was extracted.

Storage.save takes a TaskList rather than the raw ArrayList, so the
internal list is never handed out.

Behaviour is unchanged; all 58 text-UI cases pass with the test plan
untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract command parsing into a Parser class and run Thomas as an object
commitResults.messageBody:
The read loop still held every detail of the input format: splitting the
line, checking arguments, and about seventy lines of /by and /from ... /to
handling inline in a switch case. The shape of a command and the steps it
takes were tangled together, so neither could be read without the other.

Move all of it into Parser, built from one line and splitting it once. The
keyword is resolved in the constructor, so holding a Parser means holding a
real command; the arguments are parsed only when asked for, since a list
carries none. parseNewTask returns a Task, so the three add commands are
still handled together and Thomas never learns which subclass it got.

With the parsing gone, Thomas becomes what it should have been: storage,
ui and tasks as fields, a constructor that loads, and run() that
dispatches. save() no longer needs its three parameters, and main is one
line. Each case in the switch now reads as the steps its command takes.

Behaviour is unchanged; all 58 text-UI cases pass with the test plan
untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename the Command enum to CommandType
commitResults.messageBody:
The name Command is wanted for an abstract class whose subclasses carry
out commands. The enum does not carry anything out: it decides which
command a typed keyword names, and nothing else. Renaming it says so,
and frees the better name for the thing that deserves it.

Renamed with git mv so the file's history follows it. Behaviour is
unchanged; all 58 text-UI cases pass with the test plan untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace the command switch with a Command class hierarchy
commitResults.messageBody:
run() dispatched every command itself through a switch, so it held the
steps of all seven: what each one changes, when it saves, and what it
says afterwards. Adding a command meant editing that loop, and the loop
grew with every command the chatbot learned.

Add an abstract Command with execute(tasks, ui, storage) and isExit(),
and a subclass per command. Parser.parse now returns a command built
with its arguments already read, so executing does no parsing; the
range check stays in execute, since whether a task number exists cannot
be known until the list is in hand. run() reads a line, parses it, runs
it and asks whether to stop, and never learns which command it held.

Parse dispatch is a switch expression over CommandType, so the compiler
checks that every keyword has a command class. The AssertionError guard
the old switch statement needed is gone: what it caught at run time is
now caught at compile time.

The save-and-report-failure helper moves to Command as a protected
method, inherited by the four commands that change the list.

Unlike the sample code in the brief, the divider lines are not printed
around each command from run(): Ui.showBlock already wraps its own
output, so doing both would double them. showWelcome also stays in the
constructor, where it prints before loading, so a complaint about the
save file still arrives after the greeting.

Behaviour is unchanged; all 58 text-UI cases pass with the test plan
untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreOOP'
Move ThomasException and the Task family into packages
commitResults.messageBody:
First step of organising the classes into packages, with src/main/java
kept as the source root. ThomasException goes to thomas, and the four
task types to thomas.task.

These five move first because packaging has to proceed leaves-first: a
class in a named package cannot reference one in the default package,
since there is no way to import from the unnamed package. ThomasException
depends on nothing, and the Task family depends only on it, so this is
the largest group that can move while everything else stays put. The
remaining classes still compile because a default-package class may
import downward into a named one.

Moved with git mv so the history follows the files. Package declarations
added, and imports added to the eleven classes that use the moved types.
No visibility changes were needed: every type was already public, and
Task's protected fields are only used by its subclasses, which move with
it.

Behaviour is unchanged; all 58 text-UI cases pass with the test plan
untouched.

commitResults.messageBody:
First step of organising the classes into packages, with src/main/java

These five move first because packaging has to proceed leaves-first: a

Moved with git mv so the history follows the files. Package declarations
added, and imports added to the eleven classes that use the moved types.
No visibility changes were needed: every type was already public, and
Task's protected fields are only used by its subclasses, which move with

Behaviour is unchanged; all 58 text-UI cases pass with the test plan

commitResults.messageTitle: Move the commands, Parser and Thomas into packages
commitResults.messageBody:
Final step of the packaging. Command, CommandType and the seven command
subclasses go to thomas.command; Parser and Thomas join thomas. The
default package is now empty and src/main/java remains the source root.

These eleven move together because no smaller cut exists: Parser depends
on every command class, and the commands depend on TaskList, Ui and
Storage, which moved in the previous step. Splitting them would have
left Parser in the default package unable to import the commands it
builds.

The commands keep the thomas.Storage, thomas.TaskList and thomas.Ui
imports added last step, since thomas.command is a separate package.
Parser and Thomas drop theirs, now sharing a package with those classes;
Thomas is left importing only java.io.IOException and
thomas.command.Command.

MAIN_CLASS in the text-UI test runner becomes thomas.Thomas. The compile
step needed no change, as it already globbed recursively.

Behaviour is unchanged; all 58 text-UI cases pass with the test plan
untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-packages'
Merge branch 'add-gradle-support'
Setup Gradle for application task and checkstyle task
commitResults.messageBody: Include checkstyle task so that I do not have to manually do checkstyle. Also fix the mainClass for application task so that mainClass is now thomas.Thomas.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for Parser.parse
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser.parse is the first method put under JUnit because it is a pure
function of one String: it reads no file, prints nothing and keeps no
state between calls, so a case is one line in and one assertion out,
with no fixtures to set up or tear down. Storage touches the filesystem
and Ui writes to System.out, so neither tests as cleanly; the Command
classes need all three collaborators before they do anything at all.

parse is also where every rule about the shape of the input lives, so it
is the one place a broken separator or a reworded complaint can be
caught. Each case checks one of two things. A line that is understood
must yield the right Command subclass. A line that is not must throw
ThomasException carrying the message the user is meant to read, so these
tests pin the wording and not merely the fact of the failure. The
commands keep their parsed arguments private, deliberately -- nothing
but execute needs them -- so the tests assert which command was built
and leave what it does with those arguments to the text-UI plan.

42 cases, covering the argument-free commands, unknown and empty and
wrong-case keywords, and for each of todo, deadline, event, mark, unmark,
delete and on: the line that works, the missing argument, and every way
the arguments can be malformed. Several pin decisions that would
otherwise be easy to undo by accident. "standby" in a description is not
mistaken for the /by marker, which is what the separator's leading space
buys. A line that is nothing but a marker is blamed on the missing
description rather than the missing marker. Event markers written the
wrong way round are rejected instead of silently swapped. "mark 999"
still parses, because whether a task carries that number is TaskList's
to answer and not the parser's. "on 2019-12-02 1800" is refused, because
on asks about a whole day and a time there would be meaningless.

Two cases cover the event ordering check on both sides of its boundary:
a backwards event is refused and an event lasting no time is allowed.
The check is EventTask's constructor rather than parseEvent, so loading
the save file is held to it too; parse merely lets the exception
through.

No production code changes, so the text-UI suite is unaffected and the
plan needs no new cases. Gradle test passes, as does checkstyleTest.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for TaskList
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList is the second class put under JUnit, and for a plainer reason
than Parser was: two numbering schemes meet in it. The user counts tasks
from 1 and the ArrayList counts from 0, and the conversion between them
happens in requirePosition and nowhere else. An off-by-one there marks
or deletes the task next to the one asked for -- a mistake that survives
any run-through where the number typed happens to fall in the middle of
the list, which is what makes it worth pinning the ends down in tests
rather than by trying it out.

So the boundaries are tested on both sides throughout. Task 1 is
position 0 and the last task is size() rather than size() - 1; 0, a
negative number, one past the end and any number at all on an empty list
are each refused, with the message the user reads. deleteByNumber
repeats those checks and then covers what it alone does: removing closes
the gap, so deleting the middle of three must leave the third task
answering to number 2. A refused delete leaves the list as it was.

positionsOn gets the most cases, because two of its decisions are easy
to undo by accident. It returns positions in the whole list rather than
the count of matches so far, so the main case seeds non-matching tasks
before and between the matches and expects [1, 3]: numbering the matches
1, 2, 3 would give [0, 1] and fail here rather than quietly sending the
user to the wrong task. And an event covers both of its end days, so the
first and last day are tested as well as the middle and the days either
side -- the reading occursOn's comment warns about, isAfter && isBefore,
passes any test that only ever asks about the middle.

size, get and add are one-line delegations to ArrayList and are not
tested for their own sake, only used to set the other cases up and check
them. requirePosition is private and is covered through the sixteen
cases over the two methods that call it.

34 cases, for 76 in the suite. No production code changes, so the
text-UI plan is unaffected and needs no new cases. gradle test passes,
as does checkstyleTest.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for Storage and the Task family
commitResults.messageBody:
Third and last of the test commits, taking the suite to the roughly half
of the codebase where a bug costs the most. Storage goes first among
them because it is the one class where a mistake takes something the
user cannot get back: every other error is on screen and survives until
the next command, while a save file written or read wrongly loses tasks
silently, between one run and the next.

StorageTest reaches parseSavedTask through load() against a file in a
JUnit temporary folder, which is what Storage taking its path as an
argument is for -- the private decoder stays private and no case can see
another's file. Each way a line can be damaged is checked for both
halves of what should happen: the complaint it earns, and that the other
lines still loaded. That includes the strictness that is easy to mistake
for over-caution -- an exact field count rather than a minimum, and a
split that keeps trailing empty fields -- because both exist to stop a
description coming back truncated. A round-trip case saves every task
type and loads it again, which is the only kind that catches encoding
and decoding drifting apart: each side alone is self-consistent.

TaskTest covers parseDate hardest, as the one place that decides what
counts as a date, reached from both the command handling and the loader.
Its failures were already visible through ParserTest, but only its
failures: the parser puts what it returns into a private field, so
nothing had yet checked that a date which does parse parses to the right
moment. The display formats are pinned for the same reason, since mm
against MM and hh against HH go wrong in ways that still compile.

Two of those cases record behaviour rather than assert what I expected.
DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern resolves as SMART unless told otherwise, so
"2019-02-30 1800" is not refused but quietly moved to the 28th, and
"2019-12-02 2400" rolls to midnight on the 3rd. That is a real rough
edge -- the user is given a different date than the one they typed, and
told nothing -- but fixing it changes behaviour the text-UI plan covers,
so it belongs in its own commit. The two cases name what happens today
and say in a comment which one line would change it, so they become the
evidence the fix worked rather than an obstacle to it.

EventTaskTest and DeadlineTaskTest cover the two types with logic in
them. Both ends of an event count as part of it, so the first and last
day are tested and not just the middle: the reading that suggests itself
first, isAfter && isBefore, drops both ends while still passing any test
that only asks about the middle. A deadline drops the time before
comparing, so midnight and 23:59 on the due day are both tested.

Ui and the Command.execute methods are deliberately left out. Both need
output captured or all three collaborators built, and test/ui-test-plan.md
already covers exactly that end to end against the real console, so
repeating it here would cost more than it caught. TodoTask's two
one-line overrides are covered inside TaskTest and the storage
round-trip rather than given a file of their own.

One case, saveThenLoad_descriptionContainingSeparator_isSkipped, records
a known cost of the save format rather than a bug: a description holding
" | " saves, then vanishes on the next load. The strict field count is
what stops it returning truncated, so the task is lost rather than
corrupted. Recorded so that changing the format, or refusing such a
description when it is typed, is a deliberate act.

95 cases, for 171 in the suite. No production code changes, so the
text-UI plan is unaffected. gradle test passes, as does checkstyleTest.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse a description containing the save file's field separator
commitResults.messageBody:
A description holding " | " could not survive being saved. It writes a
line with an extra field, which the loader refuses rather than truncating
it, so the task was confirmed, listed, and then gone on the next start-up
-- reported as a complaint about a save file line the user had never seen.
Everything up to the loss said it had worked, which is the worst shape a
bug can have, and out of proportion to how rarely anyone types " | ".

Refuse it as it is typed instead. The loss becomes a refusal the user is
still looking at when they can do something about it, and the format is
left alone, so save files already written stay readable.

The check goes in Parser rather than in Task's constructor, which is
where the event ordering rule lives, because the two rules are reachable
by different routes. A save file can hold an event running backwards --
five well-formed fields, so the field count passes it and only the
constructor catches it -- and loading has to be held to that rule as much
as typing does. A save file cannot hold a description containing the
separator, because the field count catches that first, so the same check
in a constructor would never fire on the loading path. Typing is the only
way one can be made, so typing is where it is caught. Storage's strictness
is unchanged and stays the backstop for a file edited by hand.

Name the separator as Task.FIELD_SEPARATOR, beside the toSaveFormat that
writes it, so the parser can test for it without keeping a second copy of
the literal. Storage keeps its own spelling, since it splits on the
separator as a regular expression where the | must be escaped.

The check is contains(" | ") exactly, spaces and all, rather than a test
for a bare pipe: "a|b" and "c |d" split into no extra field and save and
load perfectly well, so refusing them would take away a character the
format has no trouble with.

TC43 tested the old behaviour and now tests the new one, and this is a
loss as well as a gain. That case was the only way to produce an
unreadable save file line through the UI, so the loader's skip-and-report
path -- one damaged line costing only its own task, the rest still
loading -- no longer has an end-to-end case. StorageTest covers it more
thoroughly than TC43 did, writing damaged files directly, but the
coverage has moved from end to end down to unit level. Both that and the
reasoning for refusing rather than escaping are recorded under "Not yet
covered" so the decision can be revisited without being re-derived.

Text-UI test plan: 59 cases pass, up from 58. TC43's expected output was
rewritten for the deliberate change in behaviour, and TC43a added for the
boundary. Five JUnit cases added to ParserTest, for 176 in the suite.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Set a JUnit coverage target and require it be kept up
commitResults.messageBody:
The testing section covered only the text-UI plan, which left the JUnit
suite with no instruction attached to it at all: nothing said which
methods were worth testing, and nothing required the tests to move when
the code did. A suite in that position drifts out of date one change at
a time, and each individual omission looks reasonable.

Set the target at the top ~50% highest-value methods, and say plainly
that it is about which methods rather than a line-coverage percentage.
The distinction matters, because the cheapest way to move a coverage
number is to test one-line delegations to ArrayList, which raises the
figure without catching anything. Rank by what a bug costs, with this
codebase's own examples: Storage highest, as the one class where a
mistake loses tasks silently between runs while every other error is on
screen and survives to the next command; Task.parseDate next, reached
from both the parser and the loader so that one bug is felt in two
places; TaskList for the conversion between the user's 1-based numbers
and the list's 0-based positions. Ui and the Command.execute methods are
named as deliberately below the line, since ui-test-plan.md already
covers exactly them end to end.

Require the JUnit tests to be updated with each change rather than
swept up afterwards, and add the gradle run to the steps before a change
counts as done. Open by saying what the two suites are each for, because
"we already have tests" is the reasoning that lets one of them rot.

Add four rules for writing tests worth having, each from something that
went wrong or nearly did while the suite was being written. Derive
expectations from the source and not from a run -- six cases failed
because a todo's toString was guessed as "[ ] x" rather than read as
"[T][ ] x", and had they been pasted from a run they would have passed
forever while checking nothing. Pin the message and not just the throw.
Test both sides of a boundary, since a mistake at the edges survives any
test that only asks about the middle. And when the code does something
unexpected, find out what it actually does before calling it wrong:
record defensible behaviour in a test that names it, with a comment
saying what would change it, or report a real bug -- but never quietly
assert buggy behaviour as correct. Finally, say when coverage moves or
is lost, since rewriting a case's expected output is a test silently
replaced unless the change says so.

CLAUDE.md is a single @AGENTS.md import and picks this up unchanged. No
code under src/ changed, so neither suite needed running.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix the checkstyleMain violations
commitResults.messageBody:
The checkstyle task has been failing on the main sources since the
config was added, on 38 violations across 16 files. A check suite that
is known to fail stops being read, and the next real violation arrives
unnoticed among the ones everybody has learned to ignore, so clear the
lot rather than the interesting ones.

Nothing here changes behaviour. All 59 text-UI cases and all 176 JUnit
cases pass unchanged.

Fifteen files did not end with a newline. Mechanical, and worth noting
that the same fault kept appearing in newly written files, so it is
something in the editing chain stripping them rather than a habit.

TaskList, Storage and Ui separated java.io, java.time and java.util with
blank lines. CustomImportOrder treats all of java.* as one group, so
those read as extra separation inside a group rather than between two.
Remove them; the blank line before the thomas.* imports stays, being a
real group boundary.

Storage indented the case labels of its switch expression one level in
from the switch. Parser writes the same construct with the labels level
with the switch, which is what this config wants, so the two files
disagreed and only Parser passed. Indent Storage's case bodies to match.

Task declared the shared date formats and parseDate above its instance
fields and constructor. That reads well -- the formats are the class's
public face and the fields are an implementation detail -- but it breaks
the fields, constructors, methods order DeclarationOrder asks for. Move
description, isDone and the constructor up rather than suppress the rule,
which leaves the order as constants, fields, constructor, parseDate, the
rest: the rule is satisfied and parseDate is still the first method, near
the formats it reads. A suppressions.xml entry would have kept the
original layout and was the alternative considered.

parseDate's Javadoc opened "Kept beside the format it reads", which stopped
being literally true once the constructor moved in between. Reword to
"Kept in the same class as", leaving the point of the sentence -- that the
reader and the format it reads cannot drift apart -- unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JUnit'
Reformat all Javadoc to the coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The comments were thorough but did not follow the standard's format, and several rules were broken everywhere rather than occasionally: not one of the 140 @param, @return and @throws descriptions ended in a period, and none were capitalized. Fix the format across all 19 classes in one pass, since a half-converted file is harder to read than either version. Put every block into the prescribed shape: a summary sentence, then any conditions as plain "If ..." sentences, then a blank line, then the tags. Method summaries now open in the third person -- Returns, Adds, Creates, Marks -- where several opened with Turns, Reads, Builds or Checks before. Field comments are one line each. Drop the inline tags. {@link} and {@code} were used throughout; the standard's example uses neither, so type and literal references are now plain prose. This also removes the two {@link} references in Command that did not resolve, since Parser and Thomas sit in a different package and were never imported there -- they had been rendering as plain text anyway, which is what a broken link costs. Drop the

paragraph markup for the same reason, which is the larger change: the class comments were multi-paragraph essays and are now a few sentences each. The rationale went with them. Where the reasoning guards against a plausible "simplification" -- why unmark is its own class rather than a boolean flag on mark, why the field count is exact rather than a minimum, why the separator check sits in the parser rather than in Task -- one compressed sentence survives; elsewhere it is gone. The inline // comments inside method bodies are untouched and still carry much of it. Also correct one British spelling, "unrecognised", the standard asking for American throughout. One change here is not a comment. Removing {@link Parser} from AddCommand's field comment left thomas.Parser imported and unused, which checkstyleMain caught, so that import is deleted. Nothing else executable changed: 176 JUnit cases and all 59 text-UI cases pass unchanged, and checkstyleMain and checkstyleTest are clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reformat the test classes' Javadoc to the coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
Follows 4944efd, which converted the main sources. The standard exempts testing code from needing header comments at all, but these classes have them, and a comment that exists should look like every other comment in the project rather than like the format the main sources have just left behind. Same conversion as before. The 50 inline tags are gone, so type and method references read as prose, and the

markup with them, which turns the multi-paragraph class comments into a few plain sentences. The helper methods gain proper tag blocks. listOf, contentsOf, deadlineOn and eventFrom in TaskListTest, and saveFile, storage, writeSaveFile and readSaveFile in StorageTest, each had a one-line summary and no tags at all; they now document every parameter and return value, which is the standard's all-or-none rule applied rather than a tag added here and there. Field comments lose their trailing periods, as the standard's single-line example shows. The per-test comments are kept, though the standard would allow dropping them. Several say why a case exists rather than what it asserts -- that parseDate resolves 2019-02-30 to the 28th rather than refusing it, that both end days of an event are tested because testing the middle alone would pass either way -- and that reasoning is not recoverable from the test name. Shortened, not deleted. One change is not a comment. Removing {@link Command} from ParserTest's class comment left thomas.command.Command imported and unused, which checkstyleTest caught, so that import is deleted. This is the same side effect the AddCommand import had in 4944efd. Nothing else changed: 176 JUnit cases and all 59 text-UI cases pass, and both checkstyle tasks are clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Write "to-do" in comments so the IDE stops flagging them as TODOs
commitResults.messageBody:
IDEs scan comments for task markers with a case-insensitive \btodo\b,
which does not know that in this project "todo" is a task type the user
types rather than a note to self. Eight comments were being listed in the
TODO tool window as outstanding work. That window is meant to hold what
is still owed, and eight permanent false entries make it useless -- a
real marker left before submission would sit unnoticed among them.

Hyphenate the prose. "to-do" does not match the word boundary the pattern
needs, and it is the better English spelling anyway. TodoTask kept this
spelling until the format pass a few commits ago rewrote some of its
comments as "todo", which is where most of these came from.

Only prose changes. The keyword literal in CommandType, the TodoTask
class name, the case TODO labels and the test strings such as
Parser.parse("todo read book") are untouched, which is why both suites
pass unchanged: 176 JUnit cases, all 59 text-UI cases, and both
checkstyle tasks clean.

Two of the eight quote what the user types -- "a bare keyword such as
todo" in Parser, and "a command such as todo read book" in Ui. Hyphenated,
those examples no longer match anything the parser accepts, since to-do
is not a keyword and fromKeyword would reject it. Rewording them to drop
the example was the alternative, and this was chosen instead, so the
examples are now illustrative rather than literal.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Require "to-do" rather than "todo" in comment prose
commitResults.messageBody:
The previous commit hyphenated the eight comments the IDE was reporting
as outstanding work. Without the rule written down, the next comment
mentioning the task type would reintroduce one, and the reason for the
odd spelling would look like a typo worth tidying up.

Record it as a third project convention, beside the two already there.
Give the reason rather than the rule alone: IDEs list any comment
matching a case-insensitive \btodo\b in their TODO window, this
project's own vocabulary collides with that marker, and enough false
entries there will hide a real marker left before submission.

State the boundary explicitly, since this is the one way the rule could
do damage. It applies to prose only. The keyword literal in CommandType,
the TodoTask class name, the TODO enum constant and test strings such as
Parser.parse("todo read book") are code, and hyphenating any of them
would break the parser while looking like an act of tidying.

Note the known cost as well. Where the prose quotes what the user types,
"to-do read book" is not a command the parser accepts, so those examples
are illustrative rather than literal. Recorded so it reads as a trade
that was made rather than as a bug in the parser worth chasing.

No code changed, so neither suite was run.

commitResults.messageTitle: Move test-case comments from Javadoc into the method bodies
commitResults.messageBody:
A @Test method's name already states the feature, the scenario and the
expected result: featureUnderTest_testScenario_expectedBehavior leaves a
header comment with nothing to say that the signature does not. Half the
cases had one anyway, so the same fact was written twice, and the coding
standard exempts testing code from header comments precisely to avoid
that.

Convert all 80 to inline // comments at the top of the body they belong
to. None is dropped, because none of them was restating the name -- the
mechanical cases never had a comment in the first place. What they hold
is the part a name cannot: why a fixture is built the way it is, what a
boundary is guarding against, where the check being tested actually
lives, and that an assertion records a rough edge rather than desired
behavior. positionsOn_severalMatches is the clearest example. Its note
explains that the non-matching tasks are seeded before and between the
matches on purpose, so a wrong implementation returns [0, 1] rather than
[1, 3] -- tidy the fixture without knowing that and the case still
passes while testing nothing.

The text is unchanged. The files were restored from HEAD and each block
transformed in place, rather than rewritten, so the wording is the same
one already reviewed; only the wrapping differs, to fit the line limit at
the deeper indent.

AGENTS.md states the rule so the next test does not reintroduce a header:
a @Test method never carries a Javadoc, and anything the name cannot hold
goes inline in the body. Class comments and helper methods are unaffected
and keep ordinary Javadoc. Also correct a rule in the same file that
would have contradicted this at once -- it asked for surprising behavior
to be recorded "in a test that names it, with a comment saying what would
change it", written when a header was still the place for that -- and six
British spellings, in a document that requires American.

176 JUnit cases and all 59 text-UI cases pass, and checkstyleTest is
clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Bring Javadoc tags in line with the coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
Every @param, @return and @throws description in the project opens in
lower case and closes without a period, and five comments use British
spelling.

The SE-EDU standard the project follows asks for the opposite: tag
descriptions capitalized and ended with a period, and American spelling
throughout, the code being meant for an international audience. Neither
rule is one checkstyle can see, so both drifted without any build
failing.

Let's capitalize and punctuate all 140 tag descriptions, and respell the
five comments. The padding that aligned descriptions into columns
collapses to a single space, which is the form the standard's own
example uses.

Inline tags such as {@link} stay as they are. The standard does not ask
for their removal, and dropping them is a separate decision.

Only comments change, so nothing moves: 176 JUnit cases and all 59
text-UI cases pass unchanged, and both checkstyle tasks stay clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project follows the SE-EDU Java coding standard at the intermediate
level, but nothing in the repository says so. The rules live on a web
page, and the parts checkstyle does not enforce are applied from memory
of what Java usually looks like.

Several of the rules differ from that default. Wrapped lines indent by
eight spaces rather than four, imports are grouped in a fixed order, and
Javadoc tag descriptions are capitalized and closed with a period. Code
written from habit gets these wrong and the build still passes.

Let's record the standard as a skill, and have AGENTS.md require it be
consulted before any Java is written or edited. Keeping it as a skill
rather than inlining it in AGENTS.md keeps the rules out of the way
until Java is actually being touched.

The skill quotes the standard's own code examples for line wrapping, the
ternary form, switch bodies, import grouping and Javadoc, since those
are where the rules are pinned down rather than described.

AGENTS.md also states what the standard means in practice: new code is
written to it from the start, code you touch is brought to it, unrelated
files are left for their own commit, and checkstyle passing is not the
same as the standard being followed. The bullet asking for Javadoc "when
the purpose is not obvious" is replaced, being weaker than the standard
it now points to.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the SE-EDU Git conventions
commitResults.messageBody:
Commit messages in this project are written to a one-line instruction to
"include enough detail to explain the rationale". That leaves the shape
of a message open, and the SE-EDU Git conventions the project follows go
well beyond it: a 72-character body wrap, an imperative subject within
72 characters, and a body that explains what and why but never how.

The vague instruction also pulls against the standard. Asking only for
enough detail encourages a message to grow, where the standard treats a
body that keeps growing as a sign the commit should be split.

Let's record the conventions as a skill covering the subject line, the
body and its five-part structure, and branch naming, and have AGENTS.md
require it be consulted before any commit message is written or any
branch named.

AGENTS.md inlines the five rules most easily got wrong, so they are
visible without loading the skill, and keeps the two existing rules on
lightweight tags and not committing unasked. The second is extended:
proposing a message is not permission to commit it.

The bodies of earlier commits in this repository wrap at about 76
characters rather than 72. Fixing those means rewriting history, two of
them already pushed, so they are left as they are.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command to search task descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
Finding a task means reading the whole list. That is fine with five
tasks and useless with fifty, and the list is the only view the chatbot
offers.

Let's add "find <keyword>", listing the tasks whose description contains
that text. It follows the shape "on" already set: TaskList answers with
the positions of the matches, and Ui numbers each by its position in the
whole list.

Numbering by list position rather than 1, 2, 3 is what makes the result
usable. The number shown is the number mark and delete take, so a user
can act on what they searched for. Numbering the matches would read more
tidily and send them to the wrong task.

Deciding what matches belongs to Task.matches, beside occursOn, so the
description stays private and the search never reads a task's displayed
form. Searching for "[T]" finds tasks with that text, not every todo.

The search is case sensitive and takes the whole argument as one phrase,
both being the simplest rules that answer the request. Ignoring case
would be friendlier and matching several keywords needs a rule for how
they combine; both are recorded under "Not yet covered".

Text-UI test plan: 64 cases pass, up from 59, with five new cases and no
existing expected output changed. 21 JUnit cases added, for 197.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Forbid AI attribution in commit messages
commitResults.messageBody:
Commits in this repository carry the user as their sole author. Nothing
says so, and the assistant harness appends a Co-Authored-By trailer and
a session link to every commit by default, so the attribution arrives
unless it is removed by hand each time.

Let's state the rule where the Git conventions live: no Co-Authored-By
trailer, no generated-with line, no session link, and no mention of
Claude, Claude Code or Anthropic in a subject or body.

Say explicitly that the rule beats any harness default, and that a
message which cannot leave the trailer out is not to be committed at
all. Without that, a session follows its default and adds the trailer
while believing it is following instructions.

Extend it past commits to anything else carrying authorship outward,
such as a pull request body or a tag message. Those would otherwise be
an obvious gap in a rule about attribution.
